difficultyRationale: Requires comparing four superficially similar refactors and recognizing which one actually changes the number of reasons each class has to change, not just its internal organization.
explanation: Extracting one collaborator per concern and injecting them is the standard SRP refactor: it isolates each reason to change into its own class while keeping the orchestrating service's own responsibility — the registration workflow — intact and unaffected by edits to email wording or audit fields.

options.text: Extract `UserValidator`, `UserRepository`, `WelcomeMailer` and `RegistrationAuditLog` as separate collaborators, each owning one concern, and have `UserRegistrationService` take them as constructor parameters to coordinate the registration flow.
options.explanation: Correct. Each extracted class now has one reason to change, and `UserRegistrationService` keeps a single, clear responsibility of its own: sequencing the steps of registration. Constructor injection makes the dependencies explicit and the service easy to test with fakes.

options.text: Keep all the logic in `register`, but split it into four private methods (`validate`, `persist`, `sendEmail`, `recordAudit`) called in sequence.
options.explanation: Private helper methods improve readability but do not change how many reasons the class has to change — a tweak to the email template or the audit schema still means editing `UserRegistrationService`; the responsibilities are still fused into one class, just renamed.

options.text: Introduce a `UserRegistrationServiceBase` abstract class that declares `validate()`, `persist()`, `sendEmail()` and `recordAudit()` as abstract methods, and have `UserRegistrationService` extend it and implement all four, so the registration workflow is split across two classes connected by inheritance instead of being written in one method.
options.explanation: Inheritance here doesn't separate the responsibilities, it just relocates the same four method bodies one level up the class hierarchy; `UserRegistrationService` still has to change for all four reasons, and the base class adds an extra layer with no stakeholder of its own.

options.text: Move `register` into the `User` entity itself as `User.registerNew(form)`, so the data and the registration behavior live together.
options.explanation: This collapses four unrelated concerns into the domain entity instead of the service, which usually makes things worse: `User` would now also need a JDBC template, a mail sender and an audit logger as dependencies, mixing a persistence-ignorant domain object with infrastructure concerns.
